title: Changing Australia: Michelle Blewitt and the war on microplastics
transcript:
Host: Well, now to changing Australia and three quarters of the rubbish found along Australia's coastline is plastic. That's according to research from the CSIRO. And the problem goes beyond bottles and bags on beaches. It's the debris entering oceans through storm water systems and the growing contamination of microplastics in rivers and estuaries, entangling and poisoning water life.
Host: In 2018, marine scientist Michelle Blüth helped to set up the Australian Microplastics Assessment Program or OzMaP, a world-first national citizen science project run by the Total Environment Centre to collect and track microplastics.
Host: She's now being recognized for her broader work in promoting sustainability and community well-being. And I'm pleased to say as my guest this morning on Changing Australia, Michelle, welcome.
Michelle Blüth: Thank you. Good morning.
Host: Now, it must feel like a different lifetime ago, but you were once upon a time training dolphins at SeaWorld until you packed up your life. What brought on this big change for you?
Michelle Blüth: Well, gosh, yes. Well, my love of marine mammals stems right back to when I was a young child living in Adelaide. Uh and uh that sort of grew very much over many years of study and pursuing my passions for working with uh the larger critters in the ocean.
Michelle Blüth: Uh and then uh life sort of took a turn following becoming a mum to my beautiful daughter. Uh and uh I decided to sort of concentrate more on sort of non-for-profit work and looking at the impacts of marine debris.
Host: When you're explaining to someone the scale of the plastic pollution problem in our waterways, how do you describe it?
Michelle Blüth: Astronomical. Uh I mean, we used to say that our saying was there's more plastics in the ocean than there are stars in the universe. And so that sort of puts it into some sort of perspective.
Michelle Blüth: Uh because obviously what is out there that we we see that's visible on our beaches and our shorelines uh is the stuff we do see, but that all breaks up into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics and that becomes more and more invisible uh and what is ingested by not only the marine animals in the environment, but also by us as well.
Host: If you were to dump the contents of some of your beach samples on a table, what are some of the things that trouble you most that you're often seeing there?
Michelle Blüth: Well, we concentrated with OzMap particularly in microplastics, which was the the plastics that are less than 5 mil in size.
Michelle Blüth: Uh and uh a lot of that was, you know, coming down storm water networks and things. What surprises me the most is the sheer volume uh that come down some of our waterways and end up on our beaches.
Michelle Blüth: And it is the breakup of other larger items that are in our environment uh that just gets washed down from cars, from people, from um industry uh that ends up in our waterways and on our beaches.
Host: What what are you seeing in particular? What are the items you see again and again?
Michelle Blüth: Well, a lot of bottle caps, depending on where you are. Uh a lot of bottle caps, obviously a lot of cigarette butts still. Uh there's still in the system plastic straws which have been out of the system for many years, but you still find them that they they rock up on beaches.
Michelle Blüth: Uh and a lot of industry pellets, which is the the basis of what plastic products are made of, uh that come down through the stormwater networks as well.
Host: So, tell me about this citizen science movement. How are uh ordinary people uh getting involved?
Michelle Blüth: Well, quite easily, if you're if you're interested person, we had with OzMap um yep, people very young to very, very old being involved. Citizen science is a an opportunity to work with scientists and follow a very strict protocol, scientific protocol, so that's the data that we collect through those those programs are scientifically valid.
Michelle Blüth: So that's what OzMap was uh worked towards from the very beginning was being able to engage local communities because we couldn't be everywhere at once as scientists.
Michelle Blüth: So by training people and teaching people the methodology that everyone's doing the same thing, we're able to collect rigorous data that can be then used for for change.
Host: So what are people collecting, Michelle? And and in what way are they collecting?
Michelle Blüth: So, for the OzMap program, we were collecting uh plastics less than five mil, we're sieving it uh in a process on the tide line. So, we're looking at what was being bought in on the last tide line.
Michelle Blüth: So, um we then train people to be able to do that and follow that strict methodology and then we would count those plastics and itemize them.
Michelle Blüth: So, we would look at whether they were from um it was hard plastic fragments or they may have been fibers from synthetic playing fields or it could have been resin pellets from industry.
Host: So, what sort of reaction do you get from industry and government when you take them the evidence about the damage of plastics pollution?
Michelle Blüth: Mixed very depending on where you are. Uh obviously the program started in Sydney um back in 2018. Uh I then moved to Adelaide in 2019, so sort of started developing the program over here in South Australia.
Michelle Blüth: Um it's been met with mixed emotions, many many councils, many governments are very keen for change and they're very interested in knowing where these hotspots are.
Michelle Blüth: Some though are probably less willing to change uh and less more willing to sort of sweep it under the carpet so to speak. Uh and so that became a bit of a frustration after a while.
Host: In what way?
Michelle Blüth: Well, just that there was a lack of motivation to want change because um it is seemed a very difficult situation to be able to change when we rely on plastic products in our everyday lives.
Michelle Blüth: And so those plastic products need to be um developed and produced, but it's the the loss of some of those items into the system that they weren't particularly interested in wanting those changes made.
Host: So, what's the answer here?
Michelle Blüth: to minimize our plastic footprint, I think, is for everybody to be aware of the plastics that they use in their lives and where it ends up, that throwing it in the bin is not just saying goodbye to it.
Michelle Blüth: It's got to go somewhere. Uh so, being more uh reliant on our recycling and so now we can do soft plastic recycling again.
Michelle Blüth: So, knowing that it's not just goodbye once it goes into the bin, so just being aware of of where our plastics go.
Host: So, where does this sit in the in the production? Is it is it to do with the plastic products themselves, the design, the waste management, the regulation? What needs to happen?
Michelle Blüth: Gosh, I think it's probably a bit of everything to be honest. Um, the design definitely because obviously there's a lot of reliance on on plastic products and so there's a lot of sort of cheaper plastics that are made that are far more brittle.
Michelle Blüth: Uh and so obviously things get broken far more easily and just get tossed away. Uh waste management as well. I mean, we do a great job with managing waste generally.
Michelle Blüth: However, there is as I said, that loss into the system uh that doesn't get managed quite as well. Um and then of course with regulations and enforcement more than anything of those losses into the system, they're not just being they're not being enforced and uh regulated as much as what I think they could be.
Host: This is a global problem because the oceans uh send material which way they want to, regardless of of borders.
Host: Um are there countries though elsewhere that are dealing with this issue better, much better than Australia is?
Michelle Blüth: Yes, I see, I think some European countries are certainly dealing with things a lot better than we are. But um, on the flip side, we're obviously dealing with things a lot better than other countries that are very close to our borders.
Host: Uh, obviously there's no borders within oceans and what what get washed gets washed in from the ocean say uh in our South Eastern Asian neighbors does make its way over to our beaches.
Host: For example, off Cocus and Christmas Islands up off WA, beautiful part of the world.
Host: I was fortunate enough to go out there a few years ago with my colleagues from Tangaroa Blue Foundation.
Host: And the the rubbish that was washing in there was astronomical. Uh a lot of it coming over from Southeast Asia and there is no tap to turn that that plastic off and that's the the difficult thing.
Host: What have you learned from working with citizen scientists and working with the results that they the data that they bring into you?
Michelle Blüth: Oh, compassion. Uh it's it's amazing to work with so many people that are very passionate about wanting change and we rely on those people throughout the whole of the country with OzMap and with citizen science as a whole.
Michelle Blüth: Uh we as scientists can't, as I said, be everywhere. So, it's really great to see people that want to make change and help uh drive that change um for the future.
Host: When you're dealing with industry, regulators, government, given the scale of this problem, do you ever feel like you're hitting your head against a brick wall?
Michelle Blüth: Yes, very much so. Yes, it it does become very frustrating um when you don't see the change that you know needs to happen uh and that the the problem is getting bigger and bigger.
Michelle Blüth: Uh and we need the voices of not only the scientists, but of the citizen scientists to help drive that change and drive that more regulation is needed and and enforcement.
Host: If people walk along the beach, they see all sorts of things. But given how small some of these microplastics are, how would you describe to people how much they're not seeing, but which is there uh nonetheless?
Michelle Blüth: Well, very yes. The as my family uh would know is that I can't go to the beach and not look down.
Michelle Blüth: Uh and uh it becomes more of a uh a picking up session sometimes and it does a leisurely walk and I'm down the beach every day.
Michelle Blüth: Um it's the problem is far greater than what we realize and there's a few places in Adelaide that you can't walk along the beach without picking up microplastics.
Michelle Blüth: Um that's just getting washed into the waterway and in and into the fish and into the birds uh and then ultimately into us as well.
Michelle Blüth: So, the problem is definitely larger than than what we know of it.
Host: Dr. Michelle Blüth, thank you very much for being my guest this morning.
Michelle Blüth: Thank you very much for having me.
Host: Dr. Michelle Blüth is the former program director of OzMap uh and now a very active volunteer in her community.
Host: uh my guest this morning on Changing Australia.
